To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the edge-generated halo is a significant source of beam halo, that the halo particles generated at the edge of the source are not trapped in the beam, that the edge-generated particles pass through the beam a few centimeters downstream of the source and that a simple model of the edge-generated halo particle trajectories is in good agreement with the simulation results.

(1) edge-generated halo particles can be removed from the beam by a simple, low cost, aperture design, (2) the aperture design is robust with respect to changes in the beam current, and (3) the aperture design does not significantly perturb the beam core, and therefore does not affect the performance of the electron gun.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of beam-generated halos in UMER and the development of a simulation tool to aid in the understanding of the halo generation and propagation.
the study of the source-generated halo particles, and in particular, with the evolution of their orbits in the beam transport system.
the following questions: (1) Can edge-generated halo particles be identified and characterized?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the source-generated halo particles are found to be generated at the edge of the emitter and pass through the centerline of the beam a distance of 1-2 mm downstream of the anodes.

the edge generated halo particles are not removed by a 1.5 cm aperture located 2 cm downstream of the anodes and that the particles do not reach the center of the vacuum chamber until a distance of 4.5 cm downstream of the edge of the anodes.
the source geometry is a significant source of halo particles and the halo particles are found to pass near the center of the ring at a short distance downstream from the anode.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the source-generated halo particles are found to be a significant source of beam halo, and the halo particles can be removed by apertures located a short distance downstream from the source.

we have identified a source of halo particles that is not present in a uniform density source and that the halo particles are generated in the region of space near the source edge and are not generated at the anode plane as previously assumed.

the source-generated halo is not a significant problem for the UMER beam, at least for the present beam parameters, and that it is possible to reduce this effect to negligible levels by modifying the anode geometry.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the halo generated near the emitter edge can be removed with a relatively simple, inexpensive, aperture.
the edge-generated halo particles have orbits that are very sensitive to small variations in the source geometry.
a simple, single-particle simulation model can be used to predict the evolution of the edge-generated halo particles.
